title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents

paper.title:
Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
for Multi-Turn Search Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it.
We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%.
We attribute this to GRPO’s credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses.
To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA 1 1 1 Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Grounded-Credit-Assignment-6320 ), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less.
Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token’s advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal.
Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) has become the dominant recipe for training multi-turn search agents that interleave reasoning, tool calls, and answer generation ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) . In the Search-R1 recipe ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , a group of rollouts is sampled for each question, each rollout is scored by whether its final answer matches the gold answer, and the group-relative advantage is broadcast to every assistant token. A search-agent rollout, however, exercises two different capabilities: acquiring evidence through search and using it to answer. A single scalar cannot tell which of the two produced the outcome. Figure 1: Outcome-only RL improves accuracy without improving grounding. (a) Share of correct answers that are supported by retrieved evidence ( SupCor /Acc) on Qwen2.5-3B. Search-R1 raises EM on every benchmark (Table 2 ) but lowers this share below the initial checkpoint (before task RL) on MuSiQue and Bamboogle; GCA restores it. (b) Token-level view of the Search-R1 run (Appendix D.1 ): share of positively credited tokens (type A A or D D rollouts) that are post-hit redundant searches or belong to ungrounded type- D D rollouts, and share of answer-finding search tokens that lie in hit-but-wrong (type B B ) rollouts. Shares are computed per rollout type and ignore homogeneous groups, whose advantage is zero. This is not a benign simplification. Figure 1 a shows that Search-R1 raises exact match on all seven benchmarks we study, yet on MuSiQue and Bamboogle the share of its correct answers that are supported by retrieved evidence falls below that of the initial checkpoint (88.3% → \to 71.8% and 84.0% → \to 42.9%): the agent increasingly answers from parametric memory. We attribute this drift to the single scalar. Under GRPO, the net advantage of the rollouts in a group that retrieved answer-bearing evidence equals a positive factor times the group’s grounding gap , the accuracy difference between rollouts with and without such evidence (Proposition 1 ). In aggregate, retrieval is thus credited only insofar as it coincides with correct answers . The token-level view shows how this credit erodes (Figure 1 b): 38–51% of the search tokens up to the first answer-bearing hit lie in rollouts that later answered incorrectly, so their negative credit offsets what such searches earn in successful rollouts, while 33–40% of positively credited tokens are redundant searches or belong to ungrounded rollouts. When the model can guess from memory, or fails to use the evidence it found, the gap shrinks or reverses, and the aggregate advantage no longer favours rollouts that found evidence, consistent with Figure 1 a. We call this credit conflation . In search, however, each capability has its own verifiable sub-outcome: whether a tool response contains the gold answer, and whether the final answer matches it. We propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which adds to each functional segment a residual whose polarity follows the sub-outcome the segment controls. GCA thus shifts part of the blame for a wrong answer from the search that found the evidence to the answer, and reduces the credit of redundant searches and of correct answers that bypass retrievable evidence. Bounded so that no token changes the sign of its advantage (Proposition 2 ), the residual reweights outcome credit by at most 10% rather than overriding it. A correction this small can still matter: it is never negative on valid search, so, unlike the outcome credit, it does not cancel across rollouts. A margin–entropy salience score concentrates the residual on decision-critical tokens, and GCA needs no auxiliary model, extra rollouts, or staged training. Our contributions are: • We identify and formalise credit conflation in outcome-reward search RL, through a grounding-gap identity and token-level evidence of misaligned credit. • We propose GCA, which corrects each segment’s credit by the verifiable sub-outcome it controls (via a first-hit proxy) with a provably sign-preserving residual whose magnitudes can be learned without loss. • On seven QA benchmarks, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B, GRPO) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B, GSPO) and raises the evidence-supported share of correct answers from 76.9% to 93.4%; ablations, learned routing, and an audit of the grounding signal show that the gains do not hinge on hand-tuned rules.

sections.heading: RL for search agents.
sections.text: Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) trains LLMs to interleave reasoning and retrieval with an exact-match reward and retrieved-token masking. Follow-up work scales the environment to the web ( Song et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) , simulates the search engine ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , trains only the searcher ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , adds evidence-quality rewards ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026a ) , or branches rollouts at high-entropy tool calls ( Dong et al., 2025 ) . These methods change the environment, the reward, or the rollout procedure, but still assign one advantage to all tokens of a trajectory or turn. GCA keeps all three fixed and changes only how the advantage is distributed over tokens.

sections.heading: Finer-grained credit assignment.
sections.text: DeSA ( Wang et al., 2025c ) decouples search and answering with a two-stage curriculum, which breaks end-to-end training and requires choosing a stage-switch checkpoint. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2025a ) rewards each turn by its information gain, MT-PPO ( Wei et al., 2025 ) adds verifiable turn-level rewards and a critic, and GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and HGPO ( He et al., 2026b ) compute step-level advantages by grouping actions that share states or histories. These methods group credit by time step or environment state; GCA groups it by the functional role of a segment, an orthogonal axis.

sections.heading: Token-level weighting.
sections.text: Wang et al. (2025b) restrict policy gradients to high-entropy “forking” tokens, and RTT ( Xu et al., 2026 ) learns a token-level relevance discriminator for instruction following. GCA uses margin and entropy only to distribute a segment residual whose sign is already fixed by the diagnosis, and requires no extra model. Appendix M compares the design choices of these methods.

sections.heading: Why a bounded residual matters.
sections.text: By Proposition 1 , the net outcome advantage of hit rollouts scales with Δ \Delta , whereas the residual that GCA adds to their vSearch tokens is non-negative ( P = + 1 P{=}{+}1 in every hit type), so its aggregate does not vanish with Δ \Delta . sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: We train Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) with GRPO and the Mixture-of-Experts Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) with GSPO in verl ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) , on the NQ+HotpotQA mixture of Search-R1 with its hyperparameters (batch size 512, 5 rollouts per prompt, learning rate 10 − 6 10^{-6} , clip ratio 0.2). All runs share the prompts and the retrieval setup (E5 ( Wang et al., 2022 ) over the 2018 Wikipedia dump, top-3 passages, at most 5 turns; temperature 1.0 in training and 0 in evaluation); GCA changes only the token-level advantage. GCA uses a KL coefficient of 5 × 10 − 3 5{\times}10^{-3} instead of 10 − 3 10^{-3} ; Search-R1 trained with the larger coefficient is not better (36.61 vs. 37.36 EM; Appendix J ). Further details are in Appendix I .

sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: Following Jin et al. (2025) , we evaluate on NQ ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) , and Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) (51,713 questions). Besides EM we report the lenient accuracy (Acc, an alias-aware substring match) of the Search-R1 evaluation script, whose correctness C ~ i \tilde{C}_{i} differs from the EM correctness C i C_{i} (Eq. 1 ). The grounding metrics are ToolHit = P ⁡ ( H = 1 ) =P(H{=}1) , HitAcc = P ⁡ ( C ~ = 1 ∣ H = 1 ) =P(\tilde{C}{=}1\mid H{=}1) , supported correctness SupCor = ToolHit ⋅ HitAcc \textsc{SupCor}=\textsc{ToolHit}\cdot\textsc{HitAcc} (which can exceed EM), and the grounded share SupCor /Acc, i.e., the fraction of correct answers backed by retrieved evidence.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Initial checkpoint + search (no task RL), IRCoT ( Trivedi et al., 2023 ) , Rejection Sampling ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , ZeroSearch ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , DeSA ( Wang et al., 2025c ) , GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , and Search-R1, which we reproduce in exactly the setting of GCA. sections.heading: 5.3 Ablation study
sections.text: The three levels of GCA are nested: routes are indexed by the diagnosed type, and salience redistributes a routed residual, so a variant with salience alone has no defined sign, and removing the diagnosis leaves no route at all ( η = 0 \eta{=}0 recovers Search-R1). We therefore run budget-matched leave-one-out ablations (Table 4 ). W/o salience replaces c i , t c_{i,t} by its per-cell mean measured on a frozen GCA rollout sample, which keeps each cell’s residual budget but removes within-cell concentration. W/o segment split merges vSearch and rSearch into one search segment whose signed coefficient preserves their token-weighted residual. Merging the search segments costs 2.75 EM and 10.9 ToolHit points and lowers all seven benchmarks, most on the multi-hop HotpotQA ( − 4.4 -4.4 ) and MuSiQue ( − 4.6 -4.6 ). Without the first-hit split, the residual can no longer separate pre-hit search from potentially redundant later search, and the grounded share falls from 93.4% to 82.0%. Removing salience keeps 81.6% of the EM gain (4.65 of 5.70 points) but loses 6.8 points of ToolHit and 5.8 points of grounded share. It hurts most on NQ, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue ( − 2.1 -2.1 to − 3.2 -3.2 EM), whereas on Bamboogle, the smallest benchmark (125 questions; ± 3.7 \pm 3.7 across seeds for GCA), the constant variant scores higher. Among the tested ablations, removing the first-hit split causes the largest drop, supporting its empirical importance for separating acquisition-related from potentially redundant search.

sections.heading: 5.5 Reliability of the grounding signal
sections.text: H H is a lexical answer-coverage signal computed on the tool responses the policy actually received (top-3 passages, truncated to 1,024 tokens). We audited all 169,615 training questions (Appendix G ): yes/no answers account for 3.23% (6.06% of HotpotQA), multiple aliases for 4.57% (alternatives, matched disjunctively), and formatting artefacts for 0.97%. As a recall test, applying the matcher to the annotated supporting documents of the 90,447 HotpotQA questions misses the alias in 3.61% of cases, and in only 0.040% once yes/no answers are excluded, all of them formatting artefacts. H H is therefore a near-perfect recall proxy for genuine evidence except for yes/no verdicts, which are inferred rather than copied. Retraining without yes/no questions changes in-domain EM by about + 0.7 +0.7 (single seed, 100 steps): this noise is mildly harmful but does not drive our gains. Moreover, by Proposition 2 a misdiagnosed rollout changes its tokens’ credit by at most 10% and never flips its sign.

sections.heading: 5.6 Training dynamics
sections.text: Figure 3 shows how grounded behaviour emerges. GCA raises SupCor and retrieval coverage without a corresponding increase in the overall hit-but-wrong rate in the reported trace. It also reaches a higher mean outcome reward, leaves fewer groups with zero reward variance (70% vs. 75% at the end of training), so that more groups carry a learning signal, and keeps actor entropy higher than Search-R1 (0.59 vs. 0.36) without the entropy explosion of oversized residuals. General tool use is preserved: on BFCL v3 the 30B model improves from 68.62 to 69.14 overall, mainly on multi-turn calls (41.12 to 44.12; Appendix L ). Appendix N shows a representative trajectory of each type.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Under outcome-reward RL, the aggregate advantage favours retrieval-hit rollouts only through the within-group grounding gap, consistent with search agents trained this way gaining accuracy without gaining grounding. GCA adds a bounded, sign-preserving residual whose polarity follows the verifiable sub-outcome of each segment and concentrates it on decision-critical tokens. Across seven QA benchmarks and two backbones it improves accuracy and, more strongly, the grounding of correct answers, without extra models, rollouts, or training stages. We expect the same recipe, namely identifying the sub-outcome each segment controls and routing a bounded residual by its polarity, to transfer to agents whose intermediate outcomes are verifiable by other means, such as evidence-entailment judges or executable tests.

sections.heading: Training-time supervision.
sections.text: H H , C C , and Retr \mathrm{Retr} are computed from gold answer aliases with a lexical matcher. H H measures answer coverage rather than semantic support: it misses yes/no answers and some comparison answers, which partly explains the low grounded share of all methods on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and it may fire on passages that mention the answer without supporting it. Templated oracle queries can miss retrievable answers; we mitigate this by setting Retr ⁡ ( x ) = 1 \mathrm{Retr}(x){=}1 whenever a rollout of the group hits. Gold answers are not needed at inference time, but applying GCA where no gold answer exists would require replacing these signals with, e.g., evidence-entailment judges or executable checks, which we have not evaluated.

sections.heading: Scope of the evaluation.
sections.text: We study two Qwen-family backbones and a single retrieval environment (E5 over the 2018 Wikipedia dump, top-3 passages, at most five turns); other model families and live web search remain untested. At 30B we retrain only Search-R1 as a baseline, so that comparison is a controlled transfer test rather than a full benchmark. Seed variance is reported only for GCA.

sections.heading: Design choices.
sections.text: One routing table is used for all benchmarks and backbones; learned magnitudes match it (§ 5.4 ), but we do not ablate every cell individually, and the salience weights ( α , β , γ ) (\alpha,\beta,\gamma) are fixed. The salience score reuses old-policy logits, and we did not measure its overhead.

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: Four trends emerge from Figs. 4 – 5 and Table 8 . (i) Even on supported-correct rollouts, post-hit redundant search grows. The within- A A share of rSearch increases overall across checkpoints, from 26.81 % 26.81\% to 32.91 % 32.91\% , following a small initial decrease to 26.41 % 26.41\% , counter to the naive expectation that successful rollouts should taper off retrieval once the answer is grounded. (ii) On ToolHit -but-wrong rollouts ( B 1 B_{1} ), the trajectory tilts away from useful search and toward redundant search. B 1 ⋅ rSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} rises overall ( 25.18 % → 33.67 % → 30.63 % → 39.37 % 25.18\%\!\to\!33.67\%\!\to\!30.63\%\!\to\!39.37\% ) while B 1 ⋅ vSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} falls overall ( 27.97 % → 29.26 % → 23.23 % → 24.59 % 27.97\%\!\to\!29.26\%\!\to\!23.23\%\!\to\!24.59\% ); the B 1 B_{1} rollouts are spending an increasing fraction of their budget on retrievals that do not change the answer outcome. (iii) B 2 B_{2} token mass collapses then rebounds. B 2 B_{2} total tokens fall from 10,303 10{,}303 (base) to 636 636 (step 300) and then climb back to 7,675 7{,}675 (step 900); the step 900 rSearch count ( 5,471 5{,}471 ) is within 9 % 9\% of the base count ( 6,006 6{,}006 ), signalling a relapse of the post-hit redundant-search pattern in timeout rollouts. (iv) Type D D tokens grow in absolute terms. D ⋅ rSearch D\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} at step 900 ( 25,893 25{,}893 ) exceeds the base ( 24,239 24{,}239 ), and D ⋅ Ans D\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} rises by ∼ 15 % \sim\!15\% over the same window; under outcome-only RL, this is the trajectory through which UnsupCor accrues positive advantage despite a failed retrieval. sections.heading: E.1 Building blocks: sampled-token margin and Top- M M entropy
sections.text: Let ℓ t = log ⁡ π θ old ​ ( y t ∣ s t ) \ell_{t}\!=\!\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{t}\!\mid\!s_{t}) denote the old-policy log-probability of the sampled token y t y_{t} at decoding step t t , and let 𝒱 \mathcal{V} denote the full vocabulary. We compute two old-policy diagnostics on every trainable assistant token.

sections.heading: Sampled-token margin δ t \delta_{t} .
sections.text: Let 𝒞 t = TopK ⁡ ( 𝒱 ∖ { y t } ) \mathcal{C}_{t}\!=\!\mathrm{TopK}(\mathcal{V}\setminus\{y_{t}\}) collect the K K highest-probability competing tokens at step t t . The competitor score is the log-mean-exp over 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} , ℓ ¯ t comp \displaystyle\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{comp}}_{t} = log ⁡ ( 1 K ​ ∑ v ∈ 𝒞 t exp ⁡ ( log ⁡ π θ old ​ ( v ∣ s t ) ) ) , \displaystyle=\log\!\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\exp(\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(v\!\mid\!s_{t}))\right), (8) K = 3 , \displaystyle K=3, and the sampled-token margin is the gap between the chosen log-prob and the competitor average, δ t = ℓ t − ℓ ¯ t comp . \delta_{t}\;=\;\ell_{t}\;-\;\bar{\ell}^{\mathrm{comp}}_{t}. (9) A small δ t \delta_{t} , whether negative or near zero, indicates that the sampled token is comparable to or weaker than the top alternatives: under the old policy, y t y_{t} was a low-confidence commitment whose informational value, if it contributed to a useful trajectory, was high relative to its sampling probability. A large δ t \delta_{t} indicates a confident commitment in which y t y_{t} dominates the competitors; if it contributed to an undesirable trajectory, the policy is overcommitted and a stronger negative residual is warranted.

sections.heading: Top- M M normalised entropy H ^ t \hat{H}_{t} .
sections.text: Let V t M = TopM ⁡ ( 𝒱 ) V_{t}^{M}\!=\!\mathrm{TopM}(\mathcal{V}) be the M M most likely tokens at step t t and let q v = π θ old ​ ( v | s t ) / ∑ u ∈ V t M π θ old ​ ( u | s t ) q_{v}\!=\!\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(v|s_{t})/\!\!\sum_{u\in V_{t}^{M}}\!\!\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(u|s_{t}) be the re-normalised top- M M distribution. We compute H ^ t = − ∑ v ∈ V t M q v log q v log ⁡ M ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , M = 32 . \hat{H}_{t}\;=\;\frac{-\sum_{v\in V_{t}^{M}}q_{v}\log q_{v}}{\log M}\;\in[0,1],\quad M=32. (10) H ^ t \hat{H}_{t} quantifies the spread of probability mass over the local alternatives. We use top- M M rather than full-vocabulary entropy because the tail of π θ old \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} contributes negligible mass to the decoding distribution but inflates the denominator of any normalised entropy; truncating at M = 32 M\!=\!32 keeps the dynamic range of H ^ t \hat{H}_{t} informative throughout training.

sections.heading: Why both signals are needed.
sections.text: The two diagnostics measure related but not interchangeable aspects of local uncertainty. H ^ t \hat{H}_{t} depends only on the shape of π θ old \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} , not on which token was sampled: it cannot distinguish a low-margin sample in a flat distribution from a high-margin sample in the same flat distribution. δ t \delta_{t} is sample-conditioned and identifies whether the chosen token is a winner against its near-neighbours, but it does not measure the breadth of the alternative set: a margin of δ t = 5 \delta_{t}\!=\!5 nats has very different implications when the next-best three tokens carry 90 % 90\% residual mass versus when they carry 5 % 5\% . Combining the two signals (§ E.2 –§ E.3 ) recovers the joint information that either signal alone discards.

sections.heading:
Fact 1 – entropy contracts more aggressively than margin on
the productive cells.
sections.text: On the cells where the policy converges to confident behaviour during RL ( A ⋅ vSearch A\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} , A ⋅ Ans A\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} , B 1 ⋅ vSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} , D ⋅ rSearch D\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} ), the bucket-mean entropy contracts by 2 2 – × 3\!\times between base and step 900 900 (e.g. A ⋅ vSearch A\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} : → 0.059 0.167\!\to\!0.059 ; A ⋅ Ans A\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} : → 0.139 0.204\!\to\!0.139 ; B 1 ⋅ vSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} : → 0.089 0.161\!\to\!0.089 ), and the high-entropy tail Pr [ H ^ t > 0.5 ] \Pr[\hat{H}_{t}\!>\!0.5] falls correspondingly (from ∼ 12 % \sim\!12\% to ∼ 2 \sim\!2 – 5 % 5\% ). Margin grows in the same regime but more slowly: the bucket mean rises by ∼ 50 \sim\!50 – 70 % 70\% on the search cells and the low-margin tail Pr [ δ t < 0 ] \Pr[\delta_{t}\!<\!0] remains in the 5 5 – 15 % 15\% band on every cell at step 900 900 . Implication : at mid-to-late training the entropy term β ​ H ^ t \beta\,\hat{H}_{t} contributes shrinking density to c t ± c_{t}^{\pm} on the productive cells, while the margin term retains a non-trivial discrimination range; the additive form ensures the salience score does not degenerate as one signal contracts.

sections.heading: Fact 2 – the failure-mode cells keep both signals alive.
sections.text: On the bottleneck cells the methodology is most concerned with – B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} , B 1 ⋅ rSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} , and B 2 B_{2} – the distributions are markedly more heterogeneous and both signals remain informative at every checkpoint. At step 900 900 , B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} retains a high-entropy tail of 16.2 % 16.2\% , a low-margin tail of 19.9 % 19.9\% , and a bucket mean δ ¯ ​ @ = 5.50 \bar{\delta}@3\!=\!5.50 – well below the productive-cell asymptote – and B 2 ⋅ rSearch B_{2}\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} shows a similar pattern ( 17.7 % 17.7\% high-entropy, 20.7 % 20.7\% low-margin). The per-token EDA examples on these cells are coherent with the methodology’s intent: the high- δ \delta , low- H ^ \hat{H} region of B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} surfaces digit / entity-suffix BPE pieces (‘9’, ‘8’, ‘0’, ‘wich’, ‘ Alb’) – the confidently-wrong year/entity commits the negative residual is designed to suppress – while the low- δ \delta , high- H ^ \hat{H} region of A ⋅ vSearch A\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} surfaces query-NL words (‘role’, ‘lineage’, ‘parent’, ‘quote’) – the exploration-relevant phrasing decisions the positive residual is designed to boost. The median-centring step in Eq. ( 11 ) explicitly normalises away the across-bucket mean shift so that d t ± d_{t}^{\pm} remains a within-bucket discriminator at every checkpoint.

sections.heading:
Fact 3 – the two signals are not redundant on any single
cell.
sections.text: Within every active bucket the per-token margin and entropy are weakly related but never collinear: e.g. on B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} at step 900 900 the high-entropy tail ( 16.2 % 16.2\% ) and the low-margin tail ( 19.9 % 19.9\% ) overlap on only ∼ 5 % \sim\!5\% of tokens (Fig. 7 together with Fig. 8 : the two distributions evolve under different dynamics). A score using only d t ± d_{t}^{\pm} would assign zero salience to the high-entropy / median-margin tokens (a substantial sub-population on the failure-mode cells), and a score using only H ^ t \hat{H}_{t} would assign zero salience to the high-margin / low-entropy tokens (the dominant sub-population on the productive cells). Implication : an additive composition with comparable weights ( α = 0.6 \alpha\!=\!0.6 , β = 0.3 \beta\!=\!0.3 ) is the minimal aggregator that gives non-zero salience to a token surfaced by either signal alone, and the small interaction weight γ = 0.1 \gamma\!=\!0.1 multiplicatively boosts the joint event without overwhelming the additive base.

sections.heading: E.5 Why the composition identifies the right tokens
sections.text: We now state the composition rule that follows from Facts 1–3 and matches the polarity table of § D .

sections.heading: P=+1 surfaces high-value low-probability tokens.
sections.text: On a positive segment S S , c t + c_{t}^{+} is large iff either (i) δ ¯ t ≪ 0 \bar{\delta}_{t}\ll 0 (the chosen token was decided against strong competitors – it was not the highest-probability candidate) or (ii) H ^ t → 1 \hat{H}_{t}\to 1 (the local distribution was flat, so even a high-margin pick had a substantial alternative-token mass) – and is maximal when both fire (multiplicative interaction term γ ​ d t + ​ H ^ t \gamma d_{t}^{+}\hat{H}_{t} ). Tokens in this regime are precisely the “high-value low-probability” candidates the residual aims to amplify: they were valuable enough to contribute to a productive trajectory ( P T , S = + 1 P_{T,S}\!=\!{+}1 holds at the trajectory level), but the old policy did not prefer them strongly under its own decoding distribution. The EDA’s top- 10 10 winners by − z ¯ ​ ( δ t ) + z ¯ ​ ( H ^ t ) -\bar{z}(\delta_{t})+\bar{z}(\hat{H}_{t}) on the active P=+1 cells are coherent with this characterisation – search-NL phrasing tokens (‘role’, ‘lineage’, ‘parent’, ‘quote’, ‘details’) on A ⋅ vSearch A\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} and B 1 ⋅ vSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{vSearch} , and entity-choice tokens (‘John’, ‘Manchester’, ‘ Casino’) on A ⋅ Ans A\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} .

sections.heading: P=-1 surfaces low-value high-probability tokens.
sections.text: On a negative segment, c t − c_{t}^{-} is large iff δ ¯ t ≫ 0 \bar{\delta}_{t}\gg 0 (the chosen token was strongly preferred over its top- K K competitors) and/or conf t → 1 \mathrm{conf}_{t}\to 1 (the local distribution was peaked). Tokens in this regime are the dual: confident commitments emitted in a trajectory that the trajectory-level signal flagged as undesirable ( P T , S = − 1 P_{T,S}\!=\!-1 ). Suppressing exactly these tokens is what distinguishes GCA’s residual from a uniform negative advantage on the segment, which would penalise low-confidence tokens equally and risk collateral damage to the formatting / structural surface of the response. The EDA’s top- 10 10 losers by z ¯ ​ ( δ t ) − z ¯ ​ ( H ^ t ) \bar{z}(\delta_{t})-\bar{z}(\hat{H}_{t}) on the active P= − 1 -1 cells confirm this: digit and proper-noun BPE pieces (‘9’, ‘8’, ‘0’, ‘wich’, ‘zej’, ‘shire’) on B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} and B 1 ⋅ rSearch B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{rSearch} – exactly the confidently-wrong year and entity commitments and the over-search filler tokens, respectively.

sections.heading: Why the additive form, not a product or a max.
sections.text: Three alternatives we considered were (a) a pure product c t = d t ± ​ H ^ t c_{t}\!=\!d_{t}^{\pm}\,\hat{H}_{t} , (b) a pure max c t = max ⁡ ( d t ± , H ^ t ) c_{t}\!=\!\max(d_{t}^{\pm},\hat{H}_{t}) , and (c) a margin-only c t = d t ± c_{t}\!=\!d_{t}^{\pm} . Form (a) is sub-additive: c t ≤ min ⁡ ( d t ± , H ^ t ) c_{t}\!\leq\!\min(d_{t}^{\pm},\hat{H}_{t}) , so the score cannot exceed the smaller of the two signals on any token. On the productive cells where the entropy mean has contracted to H ^ t ∼ 0.06 \hat{H}_{t}\!\sim\!0.06 – 0.14 0.14 at step 900 900 (Fact 1), the per-token upper bound under a pure product is below 0.15 0.15 regardless of how large d t ± d_{t}^{\pm} becomes, so the cell can never claim the full c max = 0.5 c_{\max}\!=\!0.5 residual budget even on its highest-margin tokens. Form (b) is robust to per-cell shrinkage but loses the co-firing amplification signal – the joint ( d t ± → 1 , H ^ t → 1 ) (d_{t}^{\pm}\!\to\!1,\hat{H}_{t}\!\to\!1) event identified in Fact 3 – which the EDA’s per-token examples confirm is the most polarity-aligned region. Form (c) drops the entropy term entirely and is well-defined throughout training, but leaves the high-entropy / median-margin sub-population identified in Fact 3 (e.g. ∼ 16 % \sim\!16\% of tokens on B 1 ⋅ Ans B_{1}\!\cdot\!\textsc{Ans} at step 900 900 , and ≥ 12 % \geq\!12\% of tokens on every active cell at base ) without any salience boost. The additive-with-interaction form Eqs. ( 13 )–( 15 ) is the simplest composition that (i) does not degenerate when one signal vanishes, (ii) gives the joint event a multiplicative boost, and (iii) keeps both signals’ weights interpretable as fractions of the unit budget α + β + γ = 1 \alpha+\beta+\gamma=1 .

sections.heading: Appendix F Oracle-query retrievability
sections.text: For ToolHit = 0 =0 rollouts (types C C and D D ), we separate actor failure (ineffective queries) from corpus absence (the answer is not covered by the retrieval corpus). We instantiate templated oracle queries from the gold answer aliases and submit them to the same retrieval pipeline. If the oracle queries also fail to retrieve the answer, the question is treated as a corpus miss. To avoid false negatives, we conservatively set Retr ⁡ ( x ) = 1 \mathrm{Retr}(x)=1 whenever any rollout in the group has H i = 1 H_{i}=1 , regardless of the oracle-query result. This check affects only type- D D rollouts: retrievable type- D D rollouts receive the residual penalty for unsupported correctness (§ 4.1 ), whereas non-retrievable ones are masked, so that corpus coverage gaps are not conflated with retrieval-policy errors. Masking acts only on the policy loss: masked rollouts still contribute to the group mean and standard deviation, so the advantages of the other rollouts are unaffected. In our training logs, type- D D rollouts account for 2–3% of all rollouts, groups that are entirely type D D with zero reward variance for 0.5% of groups, and groups consisting only of non-retrievable type- D D rollouts for under 0.1%.

sections.heading: Recall on annotated evidence.
sections.text: We apply the same matcher to the annotated supporting documents of the 90,447 HotpotQA training questions (53.3% of the training data). The alias is absent in 3,269 questions (3.61%); excluding yes/no answers, it is absent in 34 of 84,966 (0.040%), all formatting artefacts that Unicode or punctuation normalisation would recover. This shows high recall on genuine supporting evidence for ordinary answers; it does not measure precision on arbitrary retrieved passages, where an answer string may appear without supporting the answer. Yes/no answers are inferred verdicts and would require an evidence-entailment criterion instead.

sections.heading: Removing yes/no questions.
sections.text: We retrained Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct without yes/no questions under otherwise identical settings. After 100 training steps, in-domain EM on NQ and HotpotQA improves by about 0.7 points, while performance on the five out-of-domain benchmarks is approximately unchanged. As a single-seed, 100-step comparison, this result is only indicative.

For w/o segment split , vSearch and rSearch are merged into one search segment per type; its polarity and magnitude are fixed before training from the token-weighted signed and absolute residual means of the two segments. Answer routing, trajectory diagnosis, data, and optimisation settings are unchanged; results are in Table 4 .

sections.heading: Appendix I Training and evaluation hyperparameters
sections.text: We use the same training and evaluation splits as Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) and otherwise follow its training recipe, modifying only the token-level loss. Abstract Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it. We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. We attribute this to GRPO’s credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses. To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA 1 1 1 Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Grounded-Credit-Assignment-6320 ), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less. Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token’s advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal. Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) has become the dominant recipe for training multi-turn search agents that interleave reasoning, tool calls, and answer generation ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) . In the Search-R1 recipe ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , a group of rollouts is sampled for each question, each rollout is scored by whether its final answer matches the gold answer, and the group-relative advantage is broadcast to every assistant token. A search-agent rollout, however, exercises two different capabilities: acquiring evidence through search and using it to answer. A single scalar cannot tell which of the two produced the outcome. Figure 1: Outcome-only RL improves accuracy without improving grounding. (a) Share of correct answers that are supported by retrieved evidence ( SupCor /Acc) on Qwen2.5-3B. Search-R1 raises EM on every benchmark (Table 2 ) but lowers this share below the initial checkpoint (before task RL) on MuSiQue and Bamboogle; GCA restores it. (b) Token-level view of the Search-R1 run (Appendix D.1 ): share of positively credited tokens (type A A or D D rollouts) that are post-hit redundant searches or belong to ungrounded type- D D rollouts, and share of answer-finding search tokens that lie in hit-but-wrong (type B B ) rollouts. Shares are computed per rollout type and ignore homogeneous groups, whose advantage is zero. This is not a benign simplification. Figure 1 a shows that Search-R1 raises exact match on all seven benchmarks we study, yet on MuSiQue and Bamboogle the share of its correct answers that are supported by retrieved evidence falls below that of the initial checkpoint (88.3% → 	o 71.8% and 84.0% → 	o 42.9%): the agent increasingly answers from parametric memory. We attribute this drift to the single scalar. Under GRPO, the net advantage of the rollouts in a group that retrieved answer-bearing evidence equals a positive factor times the group’s grounding gap , the accuracy difference between rollouts with and without such evidence (Proposition 1 ). In aggregate, retrieval is thus credited only insofar as it coincides with correct answers . The token-level view shows how this credit erodes (Figure 1 b): 38–51% of the search tokens up to the first answer-bearing hit lie in rollouts that later answered incorrectly, so their negative credit offsets what such searches earn in successful rollouts, while 33–40% of positively credited tokens are redundant searches or belong to ungrounded rollouts. When the model can guess from memory, or fails to use the evidence it found, the gap shrinks or reverses, and the aggregate advantage no longer favours rollouts that found evidence, consistent with Figure 1 a. We call this credit conflation . In search, however, each capability has its own verifiable sub-outcome: whether a tool response contains the gold answer, and whether the final answer matches it. We propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which adds to each functional segment a residual whose polarity follows the sub-outcome the segment controls. GCA thus shifts part of the blame for a wrong answer from the search that found the evidence to the answer, and reduces the credit of redundant searches and of correct answers that bypass retrievable evidence. Bounded so that no token changes the sign of its advantage (Proposition 2 ), the residual reweights outcome credit by at most 10% rather than overriding it. A correction this small can still matter: it is never negative on valid search, so, unlike the outcome credit, it does not cancel across rollouts. A margin–entropy salience score concentrates the residual on decision-critical tokens, and GCA needs no auxiliary model, extra rollouts, or staged training. Our contributions are: • We identify and formalise credit conflation in outcome-reward search RL, through a grounding-gap identity and token-level evidence of misaligned credit. • We propose GCA, which corrects each segment’s credit by the verifiable sub-outcome it controls (via a first-hit proxy) with a provably sign-preserving residual whose magnitudes can be learned without loss. • On seven QA benchmarks, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B, GRPO) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B, GSPO) and raises the evidence-supported share of correct answers from 76.9% to 93.4%; ablations, learned routing, and an audit of the grounding signal show that the gains do not hinge on hand-tuned rules. 2 Related Work RL for search agents. Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) trains LLMs to interleave reasoning and retrieval with an exact-match reward and retrieved-token masking. Follow-up work scales the environment to the web ( Song et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) , simulates the search engine ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , trains only the searcher ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , adds evidence-quality rewards ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026a ) , or branches rollouts at high-entropy tool calls ( Dong et al., 2025 ) . These methods change the environment, the reward, or the rollout procedure, but still assign one advantage to all tokens of a trajectory or turn. GCA keeps all three fixed and changes only how the advantage is distributed over tokens. Finer-grained credit assignment. DeSA ( Wang et al., 2025c ) decouples search and answering with a two-stage curriculum, which breaks end-to-end training and requires choosing a stage-switch checkpoint. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2025a ) rewards each turn by its information gain, MT-PPO ( Wei et al., 2025 ) adds verifiable turn-level rewards and a critic, and GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and HGPO ( He et al., 2026b ) compute step-level advantages by grouping actions that share states or histories. These methods group credit by time step or environment state; GCA groups it by the functional role of a segment, an orthogonal axis. Token-level weighting. Wang et al. (2025b) restrict policy gradients to high-entropy “forking” tokens, and RTT ( Xu et al., 2026 ) learns a token-level relevance discriminator for instruction following. GCA uses margin and entropy only to distribute a segment residual whose sign is already fixed by the diagnosis, and requires no extra model. We audited all 169,615 training questions (Appendix G ): yes/no answers account for 3.23% (6.06% of HotpotQA), multiple aliases for 4.57% (alternatives, matched disjunctively), and formatting artefacts for 0.97%. As a recall test, applying the matcher to the annotated supporting documents of the 90,447 HotpotQA questions misses the alias in 3.61% of cases, and in only 0.040% once yes/no answers are excluded, all of them formatting artefacts. H H is therefore a near-perfect recall proxy for genuine evidence except for yes/no verdicts, which are inferred rather than copied. Retraining without yes/no questions changes in-domain EM by about + 0.7 +0.7 (single seed, 100 steps): this noise is mildly harmful but does not drive our gains. Appendix N shows a representative trajectory of each type. 6 Conclusion Under outcome-reward RL, the aggregate advantage favours retrieval-hit rollouts only through the within-group grounding gap, consistent with search agents trained this way gaining accuracy without gaining grounding. GCA adds a bounded, sign-preserving residual whose polarity follows the verifiable sub-outcome of each segment and concentrates it on decision-critical tokens. Across seven QA benchmarks and two backbones it improves accuracy and, more strongly, the grounding of correct answers, without extra models, rollouts, or training stages. We expect the same recipe, namely identifying the sub-outcome each segment controls and routing a bounded residual by its polarity, to transfer to agents whose intermediate outcomes are verifiable by other means, such as evidence-entailment judges or executable tests. Limitations Training-time supervision. H H , C C , and Retr \mathrm{Retr} are computed from gold answer aliases with a lexical matcher. H H measures answer coverage rather than semantic support: it misses yes/no answers and some comparison answers, which partly explains the low grounded share of all methods on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and it may fire on passages that mention the answer without supporting it. Templated oracle queries can miss retrievable answers; we mitigate this by setting Retr ⁡ ( x ) = 1 \mathrm{Retr}(x){=}1 whenever a rollout of the group hits. Gold answers are not needed at inference time, but applying GCA where no gold answer exists would require replacing these signals with, e.g., evidence-entailment judges or executable checks, which we have not evaluated. Scope of the evaluation. We study two Qwen-family backbones and a single retrieval environment (E5 over the 2018 Wikipedia dump, top-3 passages, at most five turns); other model families and live web search remain untested. At 30B we retrain only Search-R1 as a baseline, so that comparison is a controlled transfer test rather than a full benchmark. Seed variance is reported only for GCA. Design choices. One routing table is used for all benchmarks and backbones; learned magnitudes match it (§ 5.4 ), but we do not ablate every cell individually, and the salience weights ( α , β , γ ) (\alpha, eta,\gamma) are fixed.
